title: Scientists Listen to Animal Sounds to Help Protect Wildlife
summary:
Animals make all kinds of sounds. Birds, mammals, insects, reptiles, frogs, fish and even crustaceans call out to find mates, defend their territory or warn others. A science called bioacoustics studies how living things make, send and hear sounds, and it is becoming a powerful tool for protecting endangered species.

Scientists can strap audio recorders to trees or set them on the ocean floor. Once in place, the recorders capture sounds without disturbing wildlife. By listening, researchers can learn which species live in an area, estimate how many there are, and find where they are, which can help reduce conflicts between animals and people.

Jonathan Growcott is a biologist who studies large meat-eating animals. Finding predators in the wild is hard, and common methods involve driving for hours looking for footprints or using camera traps. Growcott wondered if scientists could listen for the animals, too. "These sounds travel many kilometers," he said.

As a PhD student at the University of Exeter in England, Growcott ran the first large-scale sound survey of African carnivores. His team placed 50 recorders across 450 square kilometers, or 175 square miles, of Nyerere National Park in Tanzania.

He started with leopards, which are secretive and active at night. Leopards make deep roars that sound like sawing wood. By placing recorders next to cameras, he matched leopards to their roars. A computer model could tell leopards apart by their roars with 93 percent accuracy.

Then he studied lions. Using artificial intelligence, he found lions make two types of roars: the familiar full-throated roar and a shorter, lower one he called an "intermediary" roar. He also built an AI tool he calls "Shazam for lions." It identified individual lions by their roars with more than 95 percent accuracy.
why_it_matters: Listening to wildlife lets scientists count and track hard-to-find animals without disturbing them, which can help protect species at risk of extinction.

background_read: Conservation scientists need to know where animals live and how many there are before they can protect them.
Large predators such as lions and leopards roam over wide areas and are often hard to spot, especially at night.
Sound can travel long distances, so recorders can pick up calls from animals that cameras never see.
Artificial intelligence can be trained on many recordings to find patterns, such as the unique features of one animal's voice.
